answer: A place I associate with wonderfully clean air is a tea estate in the hills near Sylhet, which I visited a couple of years ago during the winter. I had just spent a few days in Dhaka, so the difference in air quality was immediately noticeable and genuinely [[refreshing]]. The moment I stepped off the bus, I could not stop taking deep breaths of the cool, [[crisp]] air. It felt as though my lungs were being cleaned out after days of breathing in the capital's smog and dust. I spent my days walking through the tea gardens and chatting with some of the workers, and in the mornings I climbed a small hill to watch the sunrise over the rows of tea bushes. The fresh air made even simple activities feel [[invigorating]], and I slept better than I had in months. What made it so pleasant was the complete absence of heavy traffic, brick kilns and factories; the environment felt truly [[unpolluted]]. The endless trees and bushes all around must have helped too, and the dew on the leaves in the early morning made everything smell wonderfully green. Honestly, the experience made me realise that clean air is something we [[take for granted]], and how badly urban pollution affects us, especially children and older people like my grandparents. I came away not only feeling healthier but also more conscious of environmental issues, and now I try to walk short distances instead of taking an auto-rickshaw. It is a place I would return to just to breathe properly again.

followUps.q: Is air pollution a problem where you live?
followUps.answer: In Sirajganj it is not as bad as in Dhaka, but it is getting worse, mainly because of dust, traffic and brick kilns in the dry season. During the monsoon the air is much cleaner.

followUps.q: Would you like to live somewhere like that?
followUps.answer: For a while, yes, but perhaps not permanently. The tea gardens are quite remote, and I would miss my family and the convenience of town. A long holiday there every year would be ideal.

note: Placed the estate near Sylhet; 'coming from a polluted city' reframed as arriving from a few days in Dhaka; added activities and why the air was clean (no kilns or factories); marked existing 'take for granted'.
